warmup.q: A C program calls mmap to get 1 GB of memory and touches none of it. About how much does its RSS, the memory it has in RAM, grow?
options: About 512 MB: the kernel fills half up front
The call fails unless 1 GB of RAM is free
warmup.why: mmap only records a region of valid addresses. The kernel finds RAM for a page the first time the program touches it. In the lab box RSS stayed at 1 MB after reserving 1 GB, and grew to 1,025 MB only after one byte of every page was written.

sections.h: Every process gets private addresses, and a page table maps them to RAM
sections.html:
Run cat /proc/self/maps in the lab box and cat lists the memory it can address: its own code at aaaac13d0000, a heap, the C library, and a stack up near fffff8183000. Those addresses are virtual. Every process has its own set, two processes can keep different data at the same address, and on every load and store the hardware translates the address to a place in physical RAM.

Why not let programs use physical addresses? Try the simplest version: each program gets a slice of the Docker VM's 8 GB, and its addresses are real RAM addresses. Two programs built to use the same addresses can't both run. A bad pointer in one overwrites another program's memory, or the kernel's. And a program can't grow its heap if a neighbour sits right after it.

The next try gives each process a base and a limit: the hardware adds the base to every address and refuses any address past the limit. Every program can now start at 0 and can't reach outside its slice. But the slice must be one contiguous run of RAM. A JVM that may grow its heap to 4 GB, with 40 threads that each need a stack, has to grab one huge chunk up front, and free memory breaks into gaps too small to use.

The design every modern CPU uses cuts both sides into fixed-size pieces. Physical RAM is split into frames, virtual addresses into pages of the same size: 4 KB in the lab box, 16 KB on an Apple Silicon Mac. A per-process page table says which frame holds each virtual page, if any. Any page can live in any frame, so a 1 GB heap needs no contiguous gigabyte, and a process can't touch another's memory because the other's frames aren't in its table.

An address splits in two. With 4 KB pages the low 12 bits are the offset inside the page (2^12 = 4,096), and the rest is the virtual page number. 0xffff42401234 is byte 0x234 of virtual page 0xffff42401.

The table can't be a plain array indexed by page number. The lab box's kernel gives each process 48-bit addresses, 256 TB: that's 2^36 pages, and at 8 bytes an entry the array would need 512 GB per process. So the table is a tree. The 36 bits of page number split into four 9-bit indices. Each index picks one of 512 entries in one table, and 512 entries of 8 bytes fill exactly one 4 KB page. The root's entry points to a level 1 table, whose entry points to level 2, then level 3, whose entry holds the frame number. Tables exist only under addresses the process uses, so a small program needs only a few dozen KB of page tables. The figure walks one address.

try.title: Page size and a process's regions
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab box (docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box) and run the block below. /proc/self/maps is the region list of the process reading it, here cat itself.
Find the code, the heap, the C library and the stack. Then work out how many 4 KB pages the [heap] line spans.
try.expect:
On the Mac, 16384. In the box (addresses change on every run, because the kernel randomises where things go):

4096
aaaac13d0000-aaaac13d7000 r-xp 00000000 00:60 1051971                    /usr/bin/cat
aaaac13ef000-aaaac13f0000 r--p 0000f000 00:60 1051971                    /usr/bin/cat
aaaac13f0000-aaaac13f1000 rw-p 00010000 00:60 1051971                    /usr/bin/cat
aaaae7e64000-aaaae7e85000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [heap]
...
ffff99230000-ffff993ca000 r-xp 00000000 00:60 1055536                    /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6
...
ffff9942e000-ffff99430000 r-xp 00000000 00:00 0                          [vdso]
...
fffff8162000-fffff8183000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                          [stack]

Each line is one region: start and end address, permissions (r-xp is readable and executable code, rw-p is writable private data), then the file it comes from, if any. The heap here is 0x21000 bytes, 33 pages. The vDSO from lesson 1 is a region too.

video.title: Virtual memory: a page-table walk and a page fault

sections.h: The TLB caches translations, and its reach decides what is cheap to touch
sections.html:
Translating through four tables means four extra memory reads, each one waiting for the one before, ahead of every load or store the program asked for. A read that misses the CPU caches costs over 100 ns in the lab box (the 1 GB row in the Try-it below). Paying that four extra times per access would make every program several times slower.

So the CPU keeps a small cache of recent translations, the TLB (translation lookaside buffer): virtual page number in, frame number out, fast enough that a hit adds almost nothing. A miss costs a walk, and the walk's reads may themselves come from the CPU caches. Most accesses hit because programs reuse pages. A loop over one 4 KB page translates it once and hits 4,095 times.

The TLB is small. CPUs have a first-level TLB of a few dozen to a couple of hundred entries and a second level of a few thousand. What counts is its reach: entries times page size. Two thousand entries of 4 KB pages cover 8 MB. A program that jumps around a bigger working set, say a 64 MB hash index probed at random, misses the TLB on most accesses and pays a walk each time.

The fix is bigger pages. An entry at level 2 of the tree can map a whole 2 MB block directly, a huge page. One TLB entry then covers 512 times as much memory, and the walk is one level shorter. tlb.c visits one cache line in every page of a buffer, in random order, first with 4 KB pages and then with 2 MB pages. Both runs touch exactly the same cache lines, so the data caches behave the same and only the number of translations differs:

buffer    pages(4 KB)   4 KB pages   2 MB pages
    1 MB         256       0.9 ns       0.9 ns
   16 MB        4096      35.9 ns       7.6 ns

At 1 MB, 256 translations fit in the TLB either way. At 16 MB, 4,096 translations don't fit, and 8 do: the same work costs almost five times as much with small pages. From 256 MB up both runs are slow, because the data no longer fits in the CPU caches either.

Linux offers huge pages two ways. Transparent huge pages (THP) let the kernel use 2 MB pages for large regions on its own; the lab box's kernel has THP set to always. Reserved huge pages (hugetlbfs) are set aside by an administrator, and the JVM uses them with -XX:+UseLargePages.

try.title: Measure what a TLB miss costs
steps: os/c/l06/tlb.c builds a random chain through one cache line in each page of a buffer, then follows it 20 million times. It runs every buffer size twice: with 4 KB pages (MADV_NOHUGEPAGE) and with 2 MB pages (MADV_HUGEPAGE).
Predict where the 4 KB column jumps, then run it.
try.expect:
Timings vary with your Mac and with what else the Docker VM is doing:

buffer    pages(4 KB)   4 KB pages   2 MB pages
    1 MB         256       0.9 ns       0.9 ns
   16 MB        4096      35.9 ns       7.6 ns
   64 MB       16384      49.5 ns      18.0 ns
  256 MB       65536     123.1 ns      78.2 ns
 1024 MB      262144     193.4 ns     139.5 ns

The 4 KB column jumps between 1 MB and 16 MB, where 4,096 translations stop fitting in the TLB; the 2 MB column needs only 8 entries for 16 MB. At 256 MB and 1 GB both columns are slow because the data itself misses the CPU caches, and the gap that remains is the cost of the walks.

sections.h: A page fault is the kernel filling in the table on first touch
sections.html:
mmap of 1 GB returns in microseconds, and the process's RSS (resident set size: its memory actually in RAM) doesn't move. The kernel didn't find 262,144 free frames and fill in a quarter of a million table entries. It wrote down one region: this range of addresses is valid, readable and writable, and backed by nothing yet. Regions are what /proc/<pid>/maps lists. The table entries stay empty.

The first time the program writes to a page, the TLB misses, the walk finds an empty entry, and the CPU can't finish the instruction. It raises a page fault: an exception that jumps into the kernel. The kernel's fault handler looks the address up in the process's regions. If the address is inside a writable region, the kernel takes a free frame, fills it with zeros, writes its number into the table and returns. The CPU runs the faulting instruction again, and this time it works. The program notices nothing, except the time it took.

This is demand paging: mmap promises the memory, and the kernel delivers it one page at a time on first touch. In the lab box each fault costs about 0.5 to 1.6 µs, and touching 1 GB of 4 KB pages takes 262,144 of them. With 2 MB pages the same gigabyte takes 512. The stepper walks through one fault.

A fault the kernel can resolve from RAM, such as a fresh zeroed page or a file page already in memory, is a minor fault. A fault that has to wait for the disk is a major fault: a file page that isn't cached, or a page that was swapped out. That costs a disk read, around 0.1 ms on an SSD and more on a network disk. /usr/bin/time -v and ps -o min_flt,maj_flt report both. Minor faults are mostly a start-up and growth cost. Major faults during request handling are a latency problem.

If the address is in no region, there is nothing to fill in. The kernel sends the thread SIGSEGV, a segmentation fault. The JVM uses that on purpose: compiled Java code reads through a reference without checking for null first, and when the read faults near address 0, the JVM's signal handler turns the SIGSEGV into a NullPointerException.

frames.say: A bug loads through a null pointer. The walk fails and the kernel looks for a region, as before, but no region covers address 0, so there's nothing to fill in. The kernel sends the thread SIGSEGV, a segmentation fault. The JVM does this on purpose: compiled code reads through a reference without checking for null, and if the read faults near address 0, the JVM's signal handler turns the SIGSEGV into a NullPointerException.

try.title: Count the faults for 1 GB
steps: os/c/l06/touch.c reserves 1 GB with mmap, then writes one byte in every 4 KB page and counts its own page faults. none touches nothing; huge asks for 2 MB pages.
Predict the fault count and RSS for each of the three runs. The last line runs it under /usr/bin/time -v, which counts faults from outside.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/touch os/c/l06/touch.c /tmp/touch 1024 none /tmp/touch 1024 4k /tmp/touch 1024 huge /usr/bin/time -v /tmp/touch 1024 4k 2>&1 | grep -E "Major|Minor|Maximum resident"

try.expect:
Addresses and timings differ between runs:

reserved 1024 MB at 0xffff5fe00000, page size 4096 bytes, RSS 1 MB, page tables 44 KB
touched (none): 3 page faults in 0 ms, RSS 1 MB, page tables 44 KB
reserved 1024 MB at 0xffff62c00000, page size 4096 bytes, RSS 1 MB, page tables 40 KB
touched (4k): 262147 page faults in 129 ms (0.49 us each), RSS 1025 MB, page tables 2092 KB
reserved 1024 MB at 0xffff65200000, page size 4096 bytes, RSS 1 MB, page tables 44 KB
touched (huge): 515 page faults in 79 ms, RSS 1025 MB, page tables 2096 KB
	Maximum resident set size (kbytes): 1049880
	Major (requiring I/O) page faults: 0
	Minor (reclaiming a frame) page faults: 262216

Reserving costs nothing. Touching 1 GB costs one fault per 4 KB page, 262,144 plus 3 from printf, and the 512 new last-level tables add 2 MB of page tables. With 2 MB pages it's 512 faults (plus 3). The page tables don't shrink: Linux keeps a spare table for each huge page so it can split it back into 4 KB pages later. Major faults: 0, nothing came from disk.

refs.title: OSTEP chapter 21: Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms

sections.h: The JVM reserves gigabytes and touches megabytes
sections.html:
A JVM started with -Xmx4g reserves 4 GB of addresses for its heap at start-up, the same way touch.c reserved its gigabyte. ps shows two numbers, in KB:

  PID    VSZ   RSS COMMAND
   40 7304252 181196 java

VSZ (virtual size) is the total size of all the process's regions: 7.3 GB here, the 4 GB heap plus other reserved regions such as thread stacks (2 MB each, from lesson 3), the code cache and class metadata. RSS is what is in RAM: 181 MB. VSZ is what the process could touch; RSS is what it has touched and still holds. A container's memory limit counts pages in RAM, never reserved addresses, so watch RSS. Lesson 8 of this track takes apart what fills the rest of it.

The heap fills in by demand paging like everything else. The JVM faults in each heap page the first time it puts objects there, so a fresh JVM pays its faults during its first minutes of traffic, spread across requests. -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch makes it touch every heap page at start-up instead. With -Xms1g -Xmx1g, maximum RSS goes from 179 MB to 1,115 MB, because the whole heap is in RAM before main runs. Minor faults go from about 5,100 to anywhere between 7,900 and 56,000 in my runs. That's well under the 262,144 that 4 KB pages would need, because this kernel gives parts of the heap 2 MB pages (the -Xmx4g run had 137 MB of AnonHugePages), and how much it got changed from run to run. Start-up stayed around 0.04 s: the JVM pre-touches the heap in 4 MB chunks on its GC threads in parallel, and the run used 0.08 to 0.10 s of system time inside 0.04 s of wall time.

Turn it on for long-running services that need steady latency: the faults happen once, before the first request. It also proves the memory is there. In a container limited to 300 MB, -Xms400m started and ran fine, because it touched little of its heap. With -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch added, the kernel killed it at start-up: exit code 137, lesson 2's 128 plus SIGKILL, and oom_kill 1 in the container's memory.events. Better there, where you notice at once, than hours later when traffic finally grows the heap into the limit. The price is that RSS is the whole heap from the first second.

Last, page size isn't universal. The lab box's arm64 kernel uses 4 KB pages and macOS on Apple Silicon uses 16 KB. Code that rounds to pages, or reasons about how many pages a buffer spans, should ask the system (getconf PAGESIZE) instead of assuming 4096.

try.title: VSZ, RSS and AlwaysPreTouch in a JVM
steps: Idle allocates 64 MB of arrays and waits. Start it with -Xmx4g and compare VSZ with RSS.
Then start it twice with a 1 GB heap, without and with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, and predict how maximum RSS and the fault count change.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l06/demo/Idle.java java -Xmx4g -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l06.demo.Idle 20 & pid=$! sleep 3 ps -o pid,vsz,rss,comm -p $pid grep -E "^(Rss|AnonHugePages)" /proc/$pid/smaps_rollup kill $pid for flag in -XX:-AlwaysPreTouch -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch; do echo "== $flag" /usr/bin/time -v java -Xms1g -Xmx1g $flag -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l06.demo.Idle 0 2>&1 | grep -E "Elapsed|Minor|Maximum resident" done

try.expect:
pid 40 holds 64 MB of arrays
  PID    VSZ   RSS COMMAND
   40 7304252 181196 java
Rss:              181196 kB
AnonHugePages:    137216 kB
== -XX:-AlwaysPreTouch
	Elapsed (wall clock) time (h:mm:ss or m:ss): 0:00.04
	Maximum resident set size (kbytes): 178836
	Minor (reclaiming a frame) page faults: 5113
== -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
	Elapsed (wall clock) time (h:mm:ss or m:ss): 0:00.04
	Maximum resident set size (kbytes): 1115084
	Minor (reclaiming a frame) page faults: 41066

7.3 GB reserved, 181 MB resident, 137 MB of it in 2 MB pages. With pre-touch the JVM holds the whole 1 GB heap before main runs. The fault count moves between runs (from about 7,900 to 56,000 in mine) depending on how much of the heap gets 2 MB pages.

analogy: A page table is a hotel's room list, one per guest group. Every group's booking says "rooms 1 to 40", and the front desk's list says which real room each of those numbers means for that group, so two groups' room 12 are different rooms and nobody can walk into another group's. The TLB is the sticky note on the desk with the last few lookups, so a busy guest doesn't wait for the full list every time. Demand paging is a hotel that confirms 40 rooms but makes each one up only when the guest first opens its door. The analogy breaks on the cost of asking. A guest at the desk waits seconds; a TLB miss costs a few dozen nanoseconds, and a program makes billions of accesses, so in a computer that small cost decides whether a hash index is fast.
world: A Quarkus service in a pod with a 2 GB memory limit, started with -Xmx1536m, might show VSZ around 5 GB and RSS around 400 MB right after deploy, and RSS creeps up for the first hour as the heap's pages get touched. Alerts set on VSZ are noise; the pod's limit and the OOM killer count RSS. If you'd rather find out at deploy time that the heap doesn't fit, start with -Xms equal to -Xmx and -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch: RSS jumps to the full heap at once, and a pod that can't hold it dies before it takes traffic. The TLB shows up in in-memory structures: an exchange-rate cache or a fraud model of a few hundred MB, read at random on every authorization, misses the TLB on most lookups with 4 KB pages. Huge pages (THP, or -XX:+UseLargePages) can make those lookups noticeably faster, and it's the same reason Oracle hosts are usually set up with reserved huge pages for the database's shared memory.
mistake: Reading VSZ as memory use. A JVM with -Xmx4g shows 7.3 GB of VSZ while it holds 181 MB of RAM, so dashboards that plot VSZ or alerts set on it fire for no reason, and people cut the heap of a perfectly healthy service. VSZ counts every reserved address: the whole heap from the start, 2 MB of stack per thread, the code cache, class metadata and more. RAM is only ever spent on pages that were touched. The fix is to watch RSS (or the container's memory charge), and to remember that RSS for a JVM grows toward -Xmx over time as the heap is used, unless AlwaysPreTouch makes it jump there at once.

compare.title: Touching 1 GB with 4 KB pages and with 2 MB pages

a.label: 4 KB pages (MADV_NOHUGEPAGE)
a.title: touch.c 1024 4k
a.html:
reserved 1024 MB at 0xffff62c00000, page size 4096 bytes, RSS 1 MB, page tables 40 KB
touched (4k): 262147 page faults in 129 ms (0.49 us each), RSS 1025 MB, page tables 2092 KB

b.label: 2 MB pages (MADV_HUGEPAGE)
b.title: touch.c 1024 huge
b.html:
reserved 1024 MB at 0xffff65200000, page size 4096 bytes, RSS 1 MB, page tables 44 KB
touched (huge): 515 page faults in 79 ms, RSS 1025 MB, page tables 2096 KB

compare.note: Same gigabyte of RAM either way. Huge pages need 512 faults instead of 262,144, but the time doesn't drop by the same factor, because most of it goes to zeroing 1 GB of memory, which both runs must do. The big win comes later, in the TLB: 16 MB of this buffer needs 4,096 translations with small pages and 8 with huge ones. getconf PAGESIZE still says 4096 in both runs, because huge pages are an extra size the kernel uses for some regions, not a new base page size.

worked.title: Read a JVM's memory from outside the JVM

steps.say: Start with the two totals. VSZ is reserved address space, RSS is RAM. A big gap is normal for a JVM.
steps.code: ps -o pid,vsz,rss,min_flt,maj_flt,comm -p $pid # PID VSZ RSS MINFL MAJFL COMMAND # 40 7304252 179640 5913 0 java

steps.say: Split RSS into anonymous memory (heap, stacks, malloc) and file pages (the JDK's code and libraries, mapped from files). Add the page tables' own cost while you're there.
steps.code: grep -E '^(VmSize|VmRSS|RssAnon|RssFile|VmPTE)' /proc/$pid/status # VmSize: 7304252 kB # VmRSS: 179640 kB # RssAnon: 157792 kB # RssFile: 21848 kB # VmPTE: 692 kB

steps.say: Check how much of it sits in huge pages. With THP set to always, a JVM heap often gets 2 MB pages without asking.
steps.code: cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled # [always] madvise never grep AnonHugePages /proc/$pid/smaps_rollup # AnonHugePages: 137216 kB

steps.say: Read the faults. MINFL (5,913 at start-up) is first touches: expected while the heap grows, gone once it has. MAJFL above 0 and climbing under steady traffic means pages are coming from disk: a memory-mapped file that isn't cached, or swap. That's the number to alert on.
steps.code: watch -n 5 ps -o min_flt,maj_flt,rss -p $pid

lab.title: Build a page-table walker with a TLB
steps: Open touch-1g.txt: real output of this lesson's touch.c in the lab box. The tests replay that run on your model and compare the fault count and the page-table size.
Read Paging.kt. The constants, Region, Outcome and the Mmu counters are written for you.
Run the tests from the labs folder. All nine fail.
Write Paging.split: shift and mask, four times for the indices and once for the offset.
Write PageTable.lookup and map. map creates a Table wherever an entry is empty, and counts it in tables.
Write the Tlb: an LRU cache of capacity translations.
Write Mmu.access: TLB, then walk, then fault or segfault. Then look at the cliff test: a 64-entry TLB serves a loop over 64 pages perfectly and a loop over 65 pages not at all.
hints: Index for level l (0 is the root): ((va ushr (12 + 9 * (3 - l))) and 511).toInt(). Offset: (va and 4095).toInt().

object : LinkedHashMap<Long, Long>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<Long, Long>) = size > capacity } is a complete LRU cache: true orders entries by access, and the override evicts the oldest.
In access, count a fault or a segfault as a TLB miss too, and add Paging.LEVELS to walkReads on every miss.
The model's 516 tables are 2,064 KB. The real run grew by 2,052 KB, because the process already had a root and a level 1 table before mmap.

drill.title: Split an address by hand
drill.prompt: Split 0x0000_7f3a_1234_5678 into its four 9-bit table indices and its 12-bit offset, as Kotlin you could run. Then say how many page faults touching 256 MB costs with 4 KB pages and with 2 MB pages.

answer.html: val va = 0x0000_7f3a_1234_5678L val indices = (0 until 4).map { level -> ((va ushr (39 - 9 * level)) and 511).toInt() } val offset = (va and 4095).toInt() println(indices) // [254, 232, 145, 325] println(offset.toString(16)) // 678 // 256 MB / 4 KB = 65,536 faults; 256 MB / 2 MB = 128 faults

recap: Every process has its own virtual addresses. A per-process page table maps each 4 KB virtual page (16 KB on Apple Silicon) to a physical frame; the low 12 bits of an address are the offset.
The table is a tree: four levels of 512-entry tables, 9 bits of the address each, so a 256 TB address space needs tables only where something is mapped.
The TLB caches recent translations. Its reach is entries times page size; past it, every access pays a four-read walk. 2 MB huge pages multiply the reach by 512.
mmap only records a region. The first touch of each page is a page fault that the kernel fills with a zeroed frame: a minor fault. A major fault waits for disk; an address in no region gets SIGSEGV.
VSZ is reserved addresses, RSS is pages in RAM. A JVM reserves its whole -Xmx up front and faults the heap in as it uses it, unless -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch touches it all at start-up.

explain.prompt: A teammate sees a JVM with -Xmx8g showing VSZ of 11 GB and RSS of 900 MB and asks which number is real, and what -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch would change. Explain.
explain.answer: Both are real, but they measure different things. The JVM reserves address space for the whole 8 GB heap at start-up, plus thread stacks, the code cache and class metadata, and VSZ adds up every reserved region: 11 GB. Reserving costs no RAM. The kernel gives a page RAM only the first time it's touched, by taking a page fault, zeroing a frame and filling in the page table. RSS counts the pages that are actually in RAM, 900 MB, and that's the number the container's memory limit and the OOM killer look at. RSS will grow toward the heap size as the heap gets used. AlwaysPreTouch makes the JVM touch every heap page during start-up, so RSS would be over 8 GB from the first second, start-up does all the faulting before traffic arrives, and if the pod's limit can't hold the heap we find out at deploy time instead of during peak load.

deeper.html:
Page tables are memory too, and you can see their cost. VmPTE in /proc/<pid>/status is the size of a process's page tables. The idle JVM above had 692 KB of them. touch.c went from 44 KB to 2,092 KB after touching 1 GB, which is the rule of thumb: about 2 MB of tables per GB of memory mapped with 4 KB pages, 0.2%. A process that maps 100 GB of a file this way spends 200 MB on tables alone, and every process that maps the same file pays it again.

The lab box's kernel has THP on for everything:

$ cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
[always] madvise never

With always, any large enough anonymous region can get 2 MB pages, which is why the JVM's heap showed AnonHugePages without asking. With madvise, only regions that ask for them with madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) get them; touch.c huge and the JVM's -XX:+UseTransparentHugePages both ask that way. A kernel thread, khugepaged, also scans memory and collapses runs of 4 KB pages into 2 MB pages later. Huge pages make TLB reach much larger; the costs are memory (a region that touches one byte in a 2 MB block holds 2 MB) and occasional stalls while the kernel finds or assembles a free 2 MB block.

The other big source of page faults is mmap of files, which lesson 7 of this track covers. A file mapping's pages come from the page cache, the kernel's copy of file data (lesson 9). If the page is cached, the fault is minor and just maps it; if not, the fault is major and waits for the disk. Kafka's index files and many databases rely on exactly this, which is why a cold page cache after a restart shows up as a burst of major faults.
